standard_text: Show on a number line that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Find and interpret sums of rational numbers in real-world contexts.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to add rational numbers, show on a number line that a number and its opposite sum to zero, and interpret those sums in real contexts like temperature and money. The on-grade work builds from zero pairs and number-line distance to the computational core: adding numbers with opposite signs by subtracting their distances and keeping the sign of the number farther from zero. Students who struggle here usually carry gaps from well below grade seven, most often shaky decimal place value and weak fraction addition. Intervention should start with those foundations, rebuild the grade six skills of adding unlike-denominator fractions and decimal arithmetic, and only then return to signed numbers.

steps.rationale: The anchor of the standard: a number and its opposite sum to 0. Seeing 5 + (-5) land back at zero on the number line is the foundation every opposite-sign sum builds on.
Before computing sums, students must read the number line for distance — recognizing which expression (using absolute value) models the gap between two points.
Finding the distance between two points on opposite sides of zero adds the two distances from zero. This turns the number-line picture into arithmetic and prepares opposite-sign addition.
The computational core: add rationals with opposite signs by subtracting the distances and keeping the sign of the number farther from zero — including fractions and mixed numbers.
The At-proficiency demand: map a real-world situation (temperature, elevation, money) onto signed addition and interpret the sum in context.
The Above-proficiency synthesis: given a and b positioned on a number line, reason about the sign and size of their sum c using additive-inverse and magnitude logic.

skills.name: Read, write, and compare decimals using place value

prerequisite_skill.description: Name the value of a digit in a decimal to the hundredths and compare two decimals.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Which is greater, 0.5 or 0.35? How do you know?

skills.i_do_script: Every digit in a decimal has a place, and the place tells its size. Watch: in 3.47, the 4 sits in the tenths place, so it is worth 4 tenths, and the 7 sits in the hundredths place, worth 7 hundredths. To compare 0.5 and 0.35, I compare the tenths first: 5 tenths beats 3 tenths, so 0.5 is greater even though 35 looks bigger than 5. On a hundredths grid, 0.5 shades 50 squares and 0.35 shades only 35.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares decimals like whole numbers, ignoring place value
canonical_error.why: The student reads the digits as a whole number instead of tenths and hundredths. More digits does not mean a bigger number; the grid shows 0.5 covers more.

skills.item_template: A decimal to the hundredths. Student names a digit's place or value, compares two decimals, or writes a decimal from words or expanded form. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: What digit is in the tenths place of 3.47?
Which is greater: 0.5 or 0.35?
What is the value of the 7 in 0.72?
Write 2 + 0.3 + 0.04 as one decimal.
Which is greater: 0.8 or 0.79?
What digit is in the hundredths place of 6.09?
Order from least to greatest: 0.4, 0.04, 0.44
Write three tenths as a decimal.

redirect_script.stop: Which place are you comparing first?
redirect_script.prompt: Line up the decimal points and compare place by place, starting with the largest place. Tenths beat hundredths no matter how many digits follow.
redirect_script.praise: You compared the tenths first, that is exactly how place value works.

vocabulary.definition: The first place to the right of the decimal point; one tenth is 1/10 or 0.1.
The second place to the right of the decimal point; one hundredth is 1/100 or 0.01.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 decimal notation with a hundredths grid (tenths and hundredths as shaded squares).

worked_example_script.text: Shade 0.5 on one hundredths grid and 0.35 on another.
Which grid has more shading? So which number is greater?
0.5 shades 50 of the 100 squares; 0.35 shades 35. So 0.5 is greater. The tenths digit decides it: 5 tenths beats 3 tenths.
If a student says 0.35 is greater because 35 > 5, send them back to the grids: which covers more?
Your turn: which is greater, 0.6 or 0.58?

skills.name: Add and subtract fractions with like denominators

prerequisite_skill.description: Add and subtract fractions that already have the same denominator.

skills.i_do_script: When the denominators match, the pieces are the same size, so I just count pieces. Watch: 3/8 + 2/8 means 3 eighths plus 2 more eighths. That is 5 eighths, 5/8. The denominator names the size of the piece, so it stays 8; only the count on top changes. On a fraction bar cut into 8 pieces, I shade 3, then 2 more, and count 5 shaded.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the denominators as well as the numerators
canonical_error.why: The student treats top and bottom as separate addition problems. The denominator is a piece size, not a count; adding eighths to eighths still gives eighths.

skills.item_template: Two fractions with the same denominator, sum less than or equal to 1 or a simple subtraction. Student adds or subtracts. Short response fluency bank.

redirect_script.stop: What size are the pieces in both fractions?
redirect_script.prompt: The denominator names the piece size, and it does not change when you add. Count the pieces on top: 3 eighths plus 2 eighths is 5 eighths.
redirect_script.praise: You kept the piece size and counted the pieces, that is it.

vocabulary.definition: The top number; it counts how many pieces you have.
The bottom number; it names the size of each piece.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 fraction meaning with fraction bars (a fraction as a count of same-size pieces).

worked_example_script.text: Draw one bar cut into 8 equal pieces. Shade 3 pieces, then shade 2 more in a second color.
How many pieces are shaded in all? What size is each piece?
5 pieces are shaded and each is one eighth, so 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8. The bottom number stays 8 because the pieces never changed size.
If a student writes 5/16, point at the bar: did the pieces get smaller when we shaded more?
Your turn: what is 7/10 - 4/10?

skills.name: Add and subtract positive fractions with unlike denominators

prerequisite_skill.description: Rename fractions with a common denominator, then add or subtract.

skills.i_do_script: I cannot add 1/2 and 1/3 as they stand because the pieces are different sizes. Watch: I cut both bars into sixths. 1/2 is the same as 3/6, and 1/3 is the same as 2/6. Now the pieces match, so I count: 3 sixths plus 2 sixths is 5 sixths. Rename first so the pieces match, then add the counts.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds numerators and denominators straight across
canonical_error.why: The student adds tops and bottoms separately instead of renaming to a common denominator. Different denominators mean different piece sizes, and you cannot count pieces of different sizes together.

skills.item_template: Two positive fractions with different denominators (denominators up to 12, common denominator up to 24). Student adds or subtracts. Numeric response.

redirect_script.stop: Are the pieces the same size yet?
redirect_script.prompt: Rename both fractions so the denominators match, then count the pieces. Find a number both denominators go into, and rewrite each fraction in those pieces.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the piece sizes first, and then the count was easy.

vocabulary.definition: A shared piece size for two fractions; a number both denominators divide into.
A fraction that names the same amount with different sized pieces, like 1/2 and 3/6.

worked_example_script.text: Draw two same-length bars. Cut one in half and shade 1/2. Cut the other in thirds and shade 1/3.
Can we count these shaded pieces together as they are? Why not?
The pieces are different sizes. Cut both bars into sixths: the half becomes 3/6 and the third becomes 2/6. Now count: 5 sixths.
If a student writes 2/5, ask them to point at a fifth anywhere in the picture. There is none, so the answer cannot be fifths.
Your turn: rename and add 1/4 + 1/3.

practice_problems.stem: Ava wrote 2/3 + 1/4 = 3/7. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She added tops and bottoms straight across. Rename: 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

activities.title: Cut Until They Match
materials: Paper fraction strips (halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, twelfths)
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair gets a target sum like 1/2 + 1/3.
2. Lay the 1/2 strip and 1/3 strip end to end.
3. Find the strip size that measures both exactly (sixths) and lay it underneath.
4. Count the small pieces and write the renamed equation 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
5. Repeat with 3/4 - 1/2 and 1/4 + 1/3. Say each time: we cut until the pieces match.

activities.title: Rename Match-Up
materials: Card deck: one card per unrenamed sum, one card per renamed form
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each sum like 1/2 + 1/6 to its renamed twin like 3/6 + 1/6.
3. To claim a match, say the common denominator out loud and give the final answer.
4. Two decoy cards rename incorrectly; set them aside and explain what went wrong.

strategy_links.why: Fraction strips make 'the pieces must match before you count' visible before the renaming procedure is named.
The straight-across error is stable and predictable; finding and fixing it in worked examples confronts it directly.

questioning_prompts: Are these pieces the same size? How can you tell?
What number do both denominators go into?
What does 1/2 become when the bar is cut into sixths?
Why does the denominator stay the same once the pieces match?
Could you have used a bigger common denominator? Would the answer change?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds numerators and denominators straight across.
misconception_redirects.say: Point at the strips: can you count a half and a third together as they are? Cut both into sixths first, then count.
misconception_redirects.praise: You renamed before you counted, that is the whole skill.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds the common denominator but forgets to rename the numerators.
misconception_redirects.say: You changed the piece size, so the count has to change too. If 1/2 becomes sixths, how many sixths is it?
misconception_redirects.praise: You changed the top and bottom together, so the fraction kept its value.

quick_checks.look_for: Renames 1/2 as 3/6 and answers 4/6 or 2/3, not 2/8.

quick_checks.prompt: What is the common denominator for 1/4 and 1/6?
quick_checks.look_for: 12 (or any common multiple, with 12 recognized as the smallest).

steps.annotation: Both 2 and 3 go into 6, so cut both bars into sixths.
A half is three sixths.
A third is two sixths.
Now the pieces match, so count them.
Both 4 and 3 go into 12.
Rename both fractions as twelfths.
Add the twelfths.
State the sum.

sentence_starters: The pieces do not match, so I rename ___ and ___ as ___.
The common denominator is ___ because both ___ and ___ go into it.

skills.name: Add and subtract decimals to the hundredths

prerequisite_skill.description: Add and subtract decimals fluently by lining up place values.

skills.i_do_script: Decimals add place by place, so the decimal points must line up. Watch: for 3.6 + 1.75, I write 3.6 as 3.60 so both numbers show hundredths. Now tenths sit over tenths and hundredths over hundredths: 3.60 + 1.75 = 5.35. On a hundredths grid, 0.60 and 0.75 together fill one whole grid and 35 more squares. Lining up the points is really lining up the place values.

canonical_error.pattern: Right-aligns the digits instead of lining up the decimal points
canonical_error.example: Computes 4.2 + 0.35 by stacking 42 over 35 and gets 0.77 or 7.7
canonical_error.why: The student lines up the last digits like whole-number addition, which puts tenths under hundredths. Place values can only be added to matching place values.

skills.item_template: Add or subtract two decimals to the hundredths (sums under 20, may need one renaming or an appended zero). Numeric response, no calculator.

redirect_script.stop: Are the decimal points lined up?
redirect_script.prompt: Stack the numbers so the decimal points sit in one column, adding a zero if a place is empty. Then add each place like whole numbers.
redirect_script.praise: You lined up the places, so every digit landed where it belongs.

vocabulary.definition: The size a digit's position gives it: ones, tenths, hundredths.
Trade ten of one place for one of the next larger place, like ten tenths for one whole.

worked_example_script.text: Write 3.6 + 1.75 stacked, with the decimal points in one column and a zero appended: 3.60 over 1.75.
Why can I write 3.6 as 3.60 without changing it?
Sixty hundredths is the same as six tenths. Now add each place: 0 + 5 hundredths, 6 + 7 tenths regroups to 1 whole and 3 tenths, 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 wholes. The sum is 5.35.
If a student stacks the 6 over the 5, ask what place each digit lives in. Tenths cannot add to hundredths.
Your turn: line up and solve 5.4 - 2.65.

practice_problems.stem: Jon wrote 4.2 + 0.35 = 0.77. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: stacked 42 over 35 by the last digit
practice_problems.answer: He lined up the last digits instead of the decimal points. 4.20 + 0.35 = 4.55.

activities.title: Build It in Money
materials: Play money or drawn dollars, dimes, and pennies
activities.instructions:
1. Build 3.6 + 1.75 in money: 3 dollars 6 dimes, then 1 dollar 7 dimes 5 pennies.
2. Combine: count pennies, then dimes, trading ten dimes for a dollar.
3. Write the stacked problem next to the money and match each trade to a regroup.
4. Repeat with 5.4 - 2.65, trading a dollar for ten dimes to subtract.
5. Say each time: dimes add to dimes, pennies add to pennies.

activities.title: Spot the Slide
materials: Worked-problem slips, half correct and half misaligned
activities.instructions:
1. Deal the slips face down.
2. Flip one at a time: decide if the decimal points were lined up or if a digit slid into the wrong place.
3. For each wrong slip, name the place that got mixed (tenths added to hundredths) and fix it.
4. Sort slips into Lined Up and Slid piles; the group must agree before sorting.

content.why: Right-aligning puts the 2 tenths under the 5 hundredths, so unlike places were added.

strategy_links.why: Money and hundredths grids make place alignment concrete before the line-up-the-points rule is named.
Thinking aloud while stacking makes the invisible choice, which digit goes under which, audible and checkable.

questioning_prompts: What place is this digit in? What place is the digit under it?
Why can you write 3.6 as 3.60?
Where did the extra whole come from when the tenths added past ten?
How is trading ten dimes for a dollar the same as regrouping?
Estimate first: should 5.4 - 2.65 be more or less than 3?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student right-aligns the digits and ignores the decimal points.
misconception_redirects.say: Build both numbers in money. Can pennies add to dimes? Line up the points so each coin adds to its own kind.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched place to place, so the sum came out true.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of order.
misconception_redirects.say: In 5.4 - 2.65, you cannot take 5 hundredths from 0 without trading. Trade a tenth for ten hundredths first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You regrouped instead of flipping the digits, that keeps the value honest.

quick_checks.look_for: 1.15, with the 8 tenths added to 3 tenths, not to 5 hundredths.

steps.annotation: Append a zero so both numbers show hundredths.
Decimal points in one column puts each place over its match.
Thirteen tenths is 1 whole and 3 tenths.
Add the regrouped whole with the ones.
Append a zero so both numbers show hundredths.
Points in one column, place over place.
Subtract the hundredths; you will need to trade a tenth.
Finish the tenths and wholes and state the answer.

sentence_starters: I lined up the decimal points so that ___ adds to ___.
I traded ten ___ for one ___ when the place filled up.

skills.name: Show that a number and its opposite sum to zero
skills.i_do_script: A number plus its opposite always equals zero — they are additive inverses. On the number line, one moves you right and the other moves you the SAME distance left, landing you back at zero. Watch: 2.3 + (-2.3). Go right 2.3, then left 2.3 — back to zero. The sum is 0. It doesn't matter how messy the number is; a value and its exact opposite always cancel.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the two magnitudes instead of recognizing they cancel to zero
canonical_error.example: For 2.3 + (-2.3) writes 4.6 (adding the sizes) instead of 0
canonical_error.why: The student combines the numbers as if same-signed, missing that opposites move in opposite directions and cancel. A number plus its exact opposite is always zero.

skills.item_template: A number plus its opposite (integers, decimals, or fractions), possibly a three-term sum that cancels. Numeric response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Opposites cancel to 0. Adding the sizes gives 4.6 (the canonical error).
A number and its opposite sum to 0 regardless of order.
Fractions cancel with their opposites too.
-5/4 + 3/4 = -1/2, then + 1/2 = 0. The three terms cancel to zero.

redirect_script.stop: Are these two the SAME number with opposite signs?
redirect_script.prompt: A number and its opposite land you back at zero — one goes right, the other the same distance left. If you see a value and its exact opposite, the sum is 0. Don't add the sizes.
redirect_script.praise: You saw the opposites cancel to zero — that's the additive-inverse idea.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers that add to 0, like 7 and -7; also called opposites.
Numbers the same distance from zero on opposite sides; they sum to 0.

worked_example_script.text: Write '6 + (-6)' with a number line.
Start at 0, move right 6. Now move left 6. Where do you end up?
Back at 0. A number and its opposite are additive inverses — they cancel. The sum is 0.
If a student writes 12, ask 'did the second move go the same way or the opposite way?'
Your turn: -4.5 + 4.5. And a harder one: -3/8 + 3/8.

practice_problems.stem: A number plus its opposite equals what?
practice_problems.answer: 0 (they are additive inverses)

practice_problems.stem: Tomas evaluated -6.5 + 6.5. Find and fix his mistake.
practice_problems.answer: These are opposites, so they cancel to 0. Tomas added the sizes; instead, one moves left 6.5 and the other right 6.5, landing back at zero.

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the blank so the sum is zero: 7.8 + ___ = 0.
practice_problems.answer: -7.8 (the additive inverse)

practice_problems.stem: Is -2/5 + 2/5 + 4 equal to 4? Explain using additive inverses.
practice_problems.answer: Yes — -2/5 and 2/5 are opposites that cancel to 0, leaving 0 + 4 = 4.
practice_problems.notes: Use cancellation to simplify a longer sum.

activities.title: Find the Zero Pairs
materials: Card set of rational numbers (each has exactly one opposite in the deck)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the number cards face up.
2. Find every pair that sums to 0 (a number and its opposite).
3. To claim a pair, say 'these cancel because they're the same distance from zero on opposite sides.'
4. One card has no partner — find it and explain (it's 0, its own opposite).
5. Debrief: how do you spot an additive-inverse pair instantly?

activities.title: Cancel, Don't Combine
activities.instructions:
1. Read Tomas's claim that -6.5 + 6.5 = 13.
2. Draw the two moves on a number line: left 6.5, then right 6.5.
3. State where you land and the correct sum.
4. Write the rule for a number plus its opposite.

content.error_step: Tomas added the two sizes instead of letting the opposites cancel.
content.why: Opposites move opposite directions and cancel: the sum is 0.

strategy_links.why: Walking the two opposite moves on a physical number line makes 'they cancel to zero' concrete.
Adding opposite magnitudes is a precise error a quick find-and-fix corrects.
Choral response on 'a number plus its opposite is...' hard-wires the additive-inverse fact.

questioning_prompts: Are these the same number with opposite signs?
On the number line, do the two moves go the same way or opposite ways?
Where do you land after moving right then the same distance left?
What do we call two numbers that sum to zero?
Can you spot a canceling pair inside a longer sum?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds the two magnitudes of a number and its opposite.
misconception_redirects.say: A number and its opposite land you back at zero — one goes right, the other the same distance left. If you see a value and its exact opposite, the sum is 0. Don't add the sizes.
misconception_redirects.praise: You saw the opposites cancel to zero — that's the additive-inverse idea.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student misses a canceling pair inside a three-term sum.
misconception_redirects.say: Scan for a number and its opposite first — cancel that pair to 0, then add what's left.
misconception_redirects.praise: You canceled the opposite pair before adding — that's an efficient move.

quick_checks.look_for: 0. An answer of 16.8 diagnoses adding the magnitudes.
12 (the opposite). Any other value means the additive-inverse idea isn't solid.

sentence_starters: ___ and ___ are opposites, so they cancel to ___.
Moving right ___ then left ___ lands me back at ___.

steps.math: look for opposites: -7/3 and 4/3 don't cancel yet
steps.annotation: Scan for canceling pairs first.
Combine the fractions with a common denominator.
Now -1 and 1 are opposites — they cancel.
The whole expression is zero.
Add the like-denominator fractions first.
Simplify to a whole number.
Now add the -2 and the 2 — what do opposites give?
State the final sum.

skills.name: Write an expression for the distance between two points
skills.i_do_script: The distance between two points is always a positive amount — you can't be a negative distance apart. So the expression for a distance uses absolute value or adds up the two distances from zero. Watch points at 8 and -4. The gap is 12. An expression that gives 12 is 8 + |-4|, because |-4| is 4 and 8 + 4 = 12. The trap expression 8 + (-4) gives only 4 — that's the signed sum, not the distance.

canonical_error.pattern: Models distance as the signed sum of the two coordinates instead of using absolute value
canonical_error.example: For points at 8 and -4, picks 8 + (-4) = 4 instead of 8 + |-4| = 12
canonical_error.why: The student adds the coordinates directly, letting the negative shrink the result. Distance is never negative; the negative coordinate's distance from zero (its absolute value) must be added.

skills.item_template: Two points on a number line (one negative, one positive) and candidate expressions. Student selects the one modeling the distance. MC.

sample_items.stem: Points A and B are at 8 and -4. Which expression models the distance between them?
A point is at -3.5. Which expression gives its distance from zero?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distance from zero is the absolute value, |-3.5| = 3.5. The negative options give a negative 'distance.'

sample_items.stem: Points are at -6 and 6. Which expression models the distance between them?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The points are 12 apart; |-6| + |6| = 12. The others give 0 (the signed sum).

sample_items.stem: Points are at -2 and 5. Which expression models the distance?

redirect_script.stop: Can two points be a NEGATIVE distance apart?
redirect_script.prompt: Distance is always positive. Use absolute value: take the distance of the negative point from zero and add, or take the absolute value of the difference. A plain signed sum shrinks the gap.
redirect_script.praise: You used absolute value so the distance came out positive — that's how distance is modeled.

vocabulary.definition: The distance of a number from zero, always non-negative; written |x|.
How far apart two points are; always a positive amount (or zero).

worked_example_script.text: Mark points at 5 and -3 on a number line.
How many units apart are they? Count across zero.
From -3 to 0 is 3, and 0 to 5 is 5, so 8 apart. An expression: |5| + |-3| = 5 + 3 = 8. Or |5 - (-3)| = |8| = 8.
If a student picks 5 + (-3) = 2, ask 'is 2 how far apart they look on the line?'
Your turn: which expression gives the distance between -7 and 2?

practice_problems.stem: What is |-9|?
Can a distance be a negative number?
practice_problems.answer: No — distance is always zero or positive.

practice_problems.stem: Points at 8 and -4: which models the distance, 8 + (-4) or 8 + |-4|?
practice_problems.answer: 8 + |-4| (= 12); 8 + (-4) = 4 is the signed sum.

practice_problems.stem: Write an expression for the distance between -6 and 6.
Nadia chose an expression for the distance between 8 and -4. Find and fix her choice.
shown_work: Nadia chose '8 + (-4)' and said the distance is 4.
practice_problems.answer: 8 + (-4) = 4 is the signed sum, not the distance. The points are 12 apart. Use 8 + |-4| = 12, or |8 - (-4)| = 12.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: signed sum instead of absolute-value distance.

practice_problems.stem: Which expression gives the distance from -3.5 to zero?
practice_problems.notes: Distance from zero is absolute value.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why |5 - (-2)| and |-2 - 5| give the same distance between -2 and 5.
practice_problems.answer: |5 - (-2)| = |7| = 7 and |-2 - 5| = |-7| = 7. Absolute value ignores order, so both give the distance 7.
practice_problems.notes: Distance is symmetric; order of subtraction doesn't matter after |...|.

practice_problems.stem: Two points are 9 apart; one is at -4. Write an expression and give the other point's possible values.
practice_problems.answer: The other point is at -4 + 9 = 5 or -4 - 9 = -13; e.g., |5 - (-4)| = 9.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: use distance to find an unknown point.

activities.title: Distance or Signed Sum
materials: Card set of expressions for point pairs (some model distance, some are signed sums)
activities.instructions:
1. Each card gives two points and an expression.
2. Sort into 'Models the distance' or 'Just the signed sum.'
3. For each card, compute the value and compare to the true gap between the points.
4. Debrief: what feature makes an expression give a true (positive) distance?

activities.title: Never Negative Apart
activities.instructions:
1. Read Nadia's choice of 8 + (-4) = 4 for the distance between 8 and -4.
2. Draw the two points and count the gap.
3. Write an expression that gives the true distance.
4. Explain why distance can't come from a plain signed sum here.

content.error_step: Nadia added the coordinates directly, letting -4 shrink the result.
content.why: The gap is 12. Use absolute value: 8 + |-4| = 12 or |8 - (-4)| = 12.

strategy_links.why: Signed-sum-vs-distance is a precise confusion a find-and-fix with a number-line count resolves.
Counting the gap on a physical number line grounds the absolute-value expression.
Thinking aloud 'distance can't be negative, so use absolute value' models the check.

questioning_prompts: Can two points be a negative distance apart?
How many units apart are these points if you count across zero?
Which expression keeps the answer positive?
What does |-4| equal, and why does that matter here?
Does the order of subtraction change the distance after absolute value?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student models distance as the signed sum, letting a negative shrink it.
misconception_redirects.say: Distance is always positive. Use absolute value: take the distance of the negative point from zero and add, or take the absolute value of the difference. A plain signed sum shrinks the gap.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used absolute value so the distance came out positive — that's how distance is modeled.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes a negative distance from a subtraction like -2 - 5 = -7.
misconception_redirects.say: Wrap the difference in absolute value: |-2 - 5| = 7. Distance is the size, not the sign.
misconception_redirects.praise: You took the absolute value of the difference — now it's a real distance.

quick_checks.prompt: Which models the distance between -5 and 3: -5 + 3 or |-5| + |3|?

quick_checks.look_for: 4. An answer of -4 means absolute value isn't understood as distance.

sentence_starters: Distance can't be negative, so I use absolute value: ___.
The gap between ___ and ___ is ___ units.

worked_solution.stem: Write an expression for the distance between the points at -7 and 2, then find it.

steps.annotation: Distance is the total gap across zero.
Add each point's distance from zero.
Absolute value of the difference gives the same gap.
A positive amount, as distance must be.

faded_example.stem: Write an expression for the distance between -3 and 6, then find it.

steps.annotation: They straddle zero.
Each point's distance from zero.
Compute the sum of the two distances.
State the distance (a positive number).

skills.name: Find the distance between two points on opposite sides of zero
skills.i_do_script: When two points are on OPPOSITE sides of zero, their distance apart is the sum of how far each is from zero. Watch points at -2 1/4 and 3 3/4. The first is 2 1/4 from zero, the second is 3 3/4 from zero, and since they're on opposite sides I add: 2 1/4 + 3 3/4 = 6. If they were on the same side I'd subtract, but across zero I add the two distances.

canonical_error.pattern: Subtracts the two coordinates (or their sizes) instead of adding the distances when the points straddle zero
canonical_error.example: For points at -2 1/4 and 3 3/4, computes 3 3/4 - 2 1/4 = 1 1/2 instead of adding to get 6
canonical_error.why: The student applies the same-side subtraction rule across zero, where it doesn't hold. Points on opposite sides are the sum of their distances from zero apart, not the difference.

skills.name: Add rational numbers with opposite signs
skills.i_do_script: When two numbers have opposite signs, they partly cancel -- and zero pairs show exactly how. Model -8 + 3 with counters: eight negatives and three positives. Each positive pairs with a negative and the pair is worth ZERO, so three pairs vanish and five negatives survive: -5. The rule just counts the survivors: subtract the smaller distance from the larger (8 - 3 = 5) and keep the sign of the number that was farther from zero (the -8), because that's the side with counters left over. Another: 6 + (-10). Four negatives survive: -4.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the magnitudes of opposite-sign numbers, or keeps the wrong sign
canonical_error.example: For -8 + 3 writes -11 (adding sizes) or 5 (wrong sign) instead of -5
canonical_error.why: The student applies same-sign rules to opposite signs, or picks the sign of the first number. Opposite signs partly cancel: subtract the distances and keep the sign of the number farther from zero.

skills.item_template: A sum of two opposite-sign rationals (integers, decimals, fractions, mixed numbers), including three-term sums. Numeric response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Subtract 8 - 3 = 5; -8 is farther, so -5. Adding sizes gives -11.

redirect_script.praise: You subtracted the distances and kept the farther number's sign — that's opposite-sign addition.

vocabulary.definition: One number positive and one negative; they partly cancel when added.

skills.name: Interpret sums of rational numbers in real-world contexts
skills.i_do_script: Real-world sums come with a built-in picture -- picture the motion before translating any words. A diver is 15 meters below the surface and ascends 6: sketch the vertical line, start at -15, arrow pointing up 6. Before computing, estimate: the climb is smaller than the depth, so the diver ends still below the surface. Then the signs record what the picture shows: below is -15, ascending is +6, and -15 + 6 = -9 means 9 meters below -- matching the estimate. Word cues (up/gain/deposit positive, down/loss/withdraw negative) are shorthand for the direction of motion; if a cue ever fights the picture, trust the picture. Always read the answer's sign back into the story at the end.

canonical_error.pattern: Assigns the wrong sign to a real-world quantity, or ignores the direction words
canonical_error.example: For 'a diver 15 m below ascends 6 m' computes 15 + 6 = 21 (both positive) instead of -15 + 6 = -9
canonical_error.why: The student treats every quantity as positive, losing the direction the context sets. 'Below/down/withdraw' must become negative before adding, and the answer's sign must be read back into the context.

skills.item_template: A real-world situation with directional quantities; student translates to signed numbers, adds, and interprets the result. Numeric response (with context).

sample_items.distractor_logic: Below = -15, ascend = +6: -15 + 6 = -9. Treating both as positive gives 21.

sample_items.distractor_logic: -4 + 9 = 5 (positive is farther).

sample_items.distractor_logic: 7 + (-10) = -3; loss must be negative.

redirect_script.praise: You matched each quantity to its sign and read the result in context — that's interpreting a sum.

skills.name: Reason about sums and additive inverses with variables
skills.i_do_script: Sometimes I reason about a sum without exact numbers, using where the values sit on a number line. If a + b = 0, then b must be the opposite of a — same distance from zero, other side. If a is positive and b is negative but smaller in size, the sum c is positive but SMALLER than a, so |c| < |a|. I judge the sign and size of a sum from the positions and magnitudes, not from a calculation.

canonical_error.pattern: Reasons about the size or sign of a sum without accounting for magnitude, or confuses 'opposite' with 'equal'
canonical_error.example: For a + b = 0 concludes b = a instead of b = -a; or claims |c| = |a| when adding an opposite-sign b actually shrinks the result
canonical_error.why: The student maps 'sum to zero' to 'the numbers are equal,' or ignores that adding an opposite-sign value moves toward zero, shrinking the magnitude. Additive inverses are opposite, not equal, and opposite-sign sums are smaller than the larger addend.

skills.item_template: An abstract statement (a + b = 0, or a and b positioned on a number line) with statements to evaluate. Student selects the true ones. MC/multi-select.

sentence_starters: Since a + b = 0, b must be ___ of a, so b = ___.
___ is farther from zero, so c is ___ and |c| ___ |a|.

worked_solution.stem: a is positive, b is negative, and |b| > |a|. Determine the sign of c = a + b and compare |c| to |a|.
worked_solution.answer: c < 0, and |c| can be larger or smaller than |a| depending on b; but c is negative because b is farther from zero.

steps.math: b is farther from zero than a
steps.annotation: |b| > |a| means b dominates the sum.

steps.math: opposite signs -> subtract, keep b's sign
steps.annotation: b is negative, so c is negative.
The sign of the sum matches the farther addend.
The magnitude is what remains after the positive a cancels part of b.

faded_example.stem: a is negative, b is positive, and a + b = 0. Determine the relationship between |a| and |b|.

steps.math: a + b = 0 means a and b are opposites
steps.annotation: b = -a.

steps.math: opposites are the same distance from zero
steps.annotation: Their magnitudes match.
State the relationship between |a| and |b|.
Explain why in one sentence.

foundation.label: Foundation (Tier 3)
foundation.description: Well below grade level (grades 3-5) prerequisite skills. Start intervention here.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: One grade below (grade 6) skills that feed this standard directly.

on_grade.label: On Grade
on_grade.description: This standard's own expectations, from below proficiency up to at proficiency.

looking_forward.label: Looking Forward
looking_forward.description: Above-proficiency work and bridges to later standards.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, adding rationals with opposite signs, the At-proficiency computational core. If they pass, move up to S5 (interpret sums in context) and S6 (reason abstractly). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks unlike-denominator fraction addition and B2 checks decimal arithmetic, the two grade 6 skills signed-number work leans on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (decimal place value) and F2 (like-denominator fractions) locate the gap in grades 3-5. S1, S2, and S3 remain available to probe the standard's own zero-pair and distance groundwork.
